notes:
- On Windows the test only shows that the mode reads the same after the failed patch as before it. It cannot show that modes were restored, because Windows keeps no POSIX permission bits. The log shows 438 (0o666) where the old literal expected 384 (0o600). That is a platform limit, and the POSIX assertions carry the real check.
- I did not run a mutation check. I reasoned from the test that a restore which skips the mode would leave `secret.txt` with the default umask mode (usually 0o644), so the `0o600` assertion would fail. The `run.sh` assertion is weaker, because an overwritten file may keep its mode regardless.

evidence:
The test still fails when restore does not put the mode back on POSIX systems: On non-win32 it asserts the pre-patch modes are exactly 0o600 and 0o755, then asserts the same modes after the failed patch (codex.test.ts lines 350-353 and 370-371). I reasoned this from the test and did not mutate the code.
The test is not skipped on any platform and its assertions hold on Windows: There is no `skip` in the file, and the test body runs on every platform. Only the literal-mode check is behind `process.platform !== "win32"`. The after-patch check compares against the mode read before the patch. Windows reported 438 for `secret.txt` after the patch, and the pre-patch read should give the same value, though I did not run it there.
findings: none blocking; see notes.
